title: Chapter 9 — That The Americans Apply The Principle Of Interest Rightly Understood To Religious Matters
paragraphs: If the principle of interest rightly understood had only this world in view, it would be very inadequate. For there are many sacrifices that can only find their recompense in another. And however much ingenuity may be applied to demonstrating the utility of virtue, it will never be an easy task to make a man live rightly who has no thoughts of dying. So it is necessary to determine whether the principle of interest rightly understood is easily compatible with religious belief. The philosophers who teach this system of morals tell men that, to be happy in this life, they must watch their own passions and steadily control their excess; that lasting happiness can only be secured by renouncing a thousand transient gratifications; and that a man must perpetually triumph over himself in order to secure his own advantage. The founders of almost all religions have used the same language. The path they point out to man is the same — only the goal is more remote. Instead of placing in this world the reward of the sacrifices they impose, they transfer it to another. Nevertheless, I cannot believe that all who practice virtue from religious motives are driven only by the hope of a reward. I have known zealous Christians who constantly forgot themselves in order to work with greater ardor for the happiness of their fellow human beings, and I have heard them declare that everything they did was only to earn the blessings of a future state. I cannot help thinking they deceive themselves. I respect them too much to believe them.

Christianity does teach that a man must prefer his neighbor to himself in order to gain eternal life. But Christianity also teaches that men ought to benefit their fellow creatures for the love of God. A sublime expression! Man, searching with his intellect into the divine conception and seeing that order is the purpose of God, freely joins in carrying out the great design. And while he sacrifices his personal interests to this consummate order of all created things, he expects no other recompense than the pleasure of contemplating it. I do not believe that interest is the sole motive of religious men. But I believe that interest is the principal means religions themselves employ to govern men, and I do not doubt that in this way they reach the multitude and become popular. It is not easy to see clearly why the principle of interest rightly understood should keep aloof from religious opinions, and it seems to me easier to show why it should draw men to them. Suppose that, in order to obtain happiness in this world, a man combats his instinct on every occasion and deliberately calculates every action of his life; that, instead of yielding blindly to the impetuosity of first desires, he has learned the art of resisting them; and that he has accustomed himself to sacrifice without effort the pleasure of a moment to the lasting interest of his whole life. If such a man believes in the religion he professes, it will cost him little to submit to the restrictions it may impose. Reason herself counsels him to obey, and habit has prepared him to endure them. If he has conceived any doubts as to the object of his hopes, he will still not easily allow himself to be stopped by them. He will decide that it is wise to risk some of the advantages of this world in order to preserve his rights to the great inheritance promised him in another. "To be mistaken in believing that the Christian religion is true," says Pascal, "is no great loss to anyone; but how dreadful to be mistaken in believing it to be false!"

The Americans do not affect a brutal indifference to a future state. They affect no childish pride in despising perils they hope to escape. They therefore profess their religion without shame and without weakness. But there is generally, even in their zeal, something so indescribably tranquil, methodical, and deliberate about it that it would seem the head, far more than the heart, brings them to the foot of the altar. The Americans not only follow their religion out of interest, but they often place in this world the interest that makes them follow it. In the Middle Ages the clergy spoke of nothing but a future state; they hardly bothered to prove that a sincere Christian can be a happy man here below. But the American preachers are constantly referring to the earth, and it is only with great difficulty that they can turn their attention from it. To move their congregations, they always show them how favorable religious opinions are to freedom and public tranquility. And it is often difficult to tell from their sermons whether the principal object of religion is to procure eternal happiness in the other world, or prosperity in this one.
